source: Inspector General covert test of TSA screening (2015, as reported)
finding: DHS red teams posing as passengers got mock explosives or banned weapons through TSA checkpoints in almost every trial. Results were leaked, not published.
numbers: 67 of 70 trials missed (about 95.7%; press rounds to 95%). Dozens of busy airports, none named. One fake bomb taped to an agent's back set off an alarm but was missed in the pat-down.
quote: The numbers in these reports never look good out of context. (Sec. Johnson)
limits: Report itself was classified; figures come from officials briefed on it. TSA said the test covered only 1 of 20 security layers. No details on item mix or trial design.
agent_relevance: A red team result is a count of misses on a chosen attack set, not a rate over all attacks. Quote the layer scope with any number.

source: DHS OIG tester background (Roth, June 2015, via press)
finding: The Inspector General said the testers were OIG auditors with no special background in this kind of work. This undercut the claim that specially trained red teams beat the screeners.
numbers: Same 67 of 70 test. Fallout: acting TSA head reassigned; Secretary ordered retraining, equipment retest and more random covert tests.
limits: Seen only as a search snippet, not opened. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Tester skill sets the bar. Weak attackers that still win show a very weak defense; strong attackers that lose show little.

source: GAO (2006) Border Security: Investigators Transported Radioactive Sources Across Our Nation's Borders at Two Locations (GAO-06-939T)
finding: Undercover GAO teams bought radioactive sources by phone from a supplier using a fake company, made forged NRC papers with off-the-shelf software, and crossed two land borders at the same time.
numbers: Two ports (US-Canada, US-Mexico). Work ran Jul-Dec 2005. Portal monitors alarmed at both crossings; both teams still got through. Each team carried enough for a dirty bomb. Supplier did not challenge the purchase.
limits: Two crossings only. GAO did not judge if CBP procedure was well designed. NRC disputed the quantity estimate (its concern threshold is higher).
agent_relevance: Failure was in the human and document step after a technical alarm worked. Detection is not defense; check what happens after an alarm.

source: GAO (2006) Border Security: Investigators Transported Radioactive Sources Across Our Nation's Borders at Two Locations (GAO-06-939T)
finding: Inspectors never questioned forged documents. Corrective briefings followed within weeks.
numbers: At both sites, no CBP inspector questioned the counterfeit bill of lading or NRC license. Briefings: CBP 21 Dec 2005; NRC 12 and 24 Jan 2006.
quote: At no time did the CBP inspector question the validity of the counterfeit bill of lading or the counterfeit NRC document.
limits: Small N (2). A covert test shows a path exists, not how often it works.
agent_relevance: Verify provenance of the inputs, not only the sensor result. A checker must test what it is shown, not trust the paper trail.

source: NIST SP 800-115 Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment (2008)
finding: Defines the standard process: planning, discovery, attack, reporting. The attack phase loops back to discovery as new access gives new targets.
numbers: Four phases. Figure 5-2 shows the attack-to-discovery loopback. Appendix B gives a Rules of Engagement template.
limits: Guide, not an experiment. Dated 2008.
agent_relevance: Same loop our schema uses: probe, learn, probe again. Rules of engagement map to explicit scope and stop rules for the agent.

source: NIST SP 800-115 Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment (2008)
finding: Separates overt (white hat: staff know and help) from covert (black hat: only upper management knows, optional trusted third party mediates). Overt teaches staff; covert tests response.
numbers: Covert testing is stated not to test every control or find every vulnerability, and is often time consuming and costly.
quote: does not focus on identifying vulnerabilities
limits: Narrative definition. No outcome data.
agent_relevance: A covert pass is evidence only about the tested path (guardrail G3: a pass must be on something not fitted).

source: Defense Science Board (2003) Task Force on the Role and Status of DoD Red Teaming Activities
finding: Report treats red teams as challenging organisational norms. Secondary summaries list failure modes: not serious tasking, lost independence, cut off from decisions.
numbers: No numbers found. Co-chairs Gold and Hermann (via DSB newsletter snippet).
limits: PDF blocked (DTIC returned HTML, FAS challenge). Only secondary summaries read; unopened.
agent_relevance: Red team value depends on independence and access to the decision maker; our critic must not share the author's context.

source: Deng et al. (2023) PentestGPT: Evaluating and Harnessing LLMs for Automated Penetration Testing
finding: Benchmark of 13 real targets with 182 sub-tasks in 26 categories. Plain LLMs do well on single steps but lose the thread of the whole test.
limits: Human expert executes commands and feeds results back; 2023 models; targets from HackTheBox/VulnHub.
agent_relevance: Single-agent long-horizon failure is context loss. Supports a program-held task state instead of the model's memory.

source: Deng et al. (2023) PentestGPT: Evaluating and Harnessing LLMs for Automated Penetration Testing
finding: Success drops sharply with difficulty. Failures are dominated by lost context, deadlocks and code misreading.
numbers: GPT-4 on easy 4/7 targets (55/77 sub-tasks); medium 1/4 (30/71); hard 0/2 (10/34). Failure reasons across 3 LLMs: session context lost 74, deadlock operations 45, false source-code interpretation 37.
limits: Counts are failed trials pooled over models.
agent_relevance: Deadlock (repeating the same step) is an impasse signal for G1. Code should detect it, not the model.

source: Deng et al. (2023) PentestGPT: Evaluating and Harnessing LLMs for Automated Penetration Testing
finding: PentestGPT splits work into reasoning, generation and parsing modules and keeps a Pentesting Task Tree held outside the model's chat.
numbers: Sub-task completion up 228.6% over GPT-3.5 and 58.6% over GPT-4 when each runs inside PentestGPT vs used directly.
limits: Semi-automated (human runs tools); gains are relative to weak baselines.
agent_relevance: Closest design match to our schema: program holds the tree, model fills one slot at a time.

source: Fang et al. (2024) LLM Agents can Autonomously Exploit One-day Vulnerabilities
finding: A GPT-4 agent with tools exploited most of 15 real one-day vulnerabilities when given the CVE text. Every other model and the scanners scored 0%.
numbers: 87% (13/15) GPT-4 with CVE description; 0% for GPT-3.5, open models, ZAP and Metasploit; 11 of 15 were past GPT-4's cutoff. Cost $3.52 per run vs about $25 estimated human labour at 30 min each.
limits: Tiny set (15), only GPT-4, manual success check, cost is an estimate.
agent_relevance: An informed attacker (told the weakness) is a far stronger red team than a blind one. State what the attacker knows.

source: Fang et al. (2024) LLM Agents can Autonomously Exploit One-day Vulnerabilities
finding: Without the CVE description success collapses, yet the agent takes about the same number of actions.
numbers: 7% (1/15) without description. Actions 24.3 with vs 21.3 without.
limits: Same 15 items.
agent_relevance: Search effort did not rise; the bottleneck is knowing where to look, not trying more. Cuts against just sampling more.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Teams of LLM Agents can Exploit Zero-Day Vulnerabilities (HPTSA)
finding: A planning agent that explores the site and launches task-specific sub-agents beats a single agent on 14 real vulnerabilities (zero-day setting).
numbers: HPTSA pass@5 42%, pass@1 18%; within 1.8x of a GPT-4 agent given the vulnerability description; up to 4.3x better than prior frameworks.
limits: 14 vulnerabilities, all past model cutoff; pass@5 is a lenient metric; GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Planner plus specialist workers is a fit for operators O1-O8, but absolute gain is modest and needs a reliable planner.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Cybench: A Framework for Evaluating Cybersecurity Capabilities and Risks of Language Models (ICLR 2025)
finding: 40 professional CTF tasks from 4 competitions, with subtasks for partial credit. Agent success tracks how long humans took to first solve.
numbers: 8 models tested. Unguided, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 17.5%; four models solve a task with first-solve-time 11 minutes; hardest task took humans 24 h 54 min. Best subtask performance 46.8% (o1-preview per text).
limits: CTFs are puzzles, not live networks. Single attempt in main table; max of 3 for scaffold comparison.
agent_relevance: Human first-solve time is a usable difficulty scale for our own tasks. Subtask credit shows partial progress is real but fails to chain.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Cybench: A Framework for Evaluating Cybersecurity Capabilities and Risks of Language Models (ICLR 2025)
finding: Scaffold effects depend on the model. Pseudoterminal and web search lifted some runs, not all.
numbers: Scaffold comparison (best of 3), unguided: pseudoterminal 20.0%, web search 20.0%, structured bash 17.5%, action-only 12.5% for the first model block (Claude 3.5 Sonnet per text); second block shows 10.0% to 15.0%.
limits: Table layout split in text extraction; row-to-model mapping partly inferred.
agent_relevance: Scaffold gains are model-specific; test each scaffold choice on our model before adopting.

source: Singer et al. (2025) Incalmo: An Autonomous LLM-assisted System for Red Teaming Multi-Host Networks
finding: Existing LLM red-team systems fail in multi-host networks because they issue irrelevant commands. A layer of high-level tasks run by code fixes much of it.
numbers: MHBench: 40 networks of 22-50 hosts. Incalmo succeeded in 37/40; best prior LLM-assisted systems 3/40. Attacks took 12-54 min and cost about $15 or less. Irrelevant commands 47-90% in the ExpertPromptShell baseline.
limits: Emulated networks, not live; authors built both benchmark and system.
agent_relevance: Strong support for code decides, model fills a slot: abstraction layer beats raw shell, 37 vs 3.

source: Lin et al. (2025/26) Comparing AI Agents to Cybersecurity Professionals in Real-World Penetration Testing (ARTEMIS)
finding: First live test: 10 professionals vs 6 existing agents vs ARTEMIS on a real university network. ARTEMIS placed second.
numbers: About 8,000 hosts, 12 subnets. ARTEMIS: 9 valid vulnerabilities, 82% valid submission rate, beat 9 of 10 humans. Humans found 3 to 13 valid vulnerabilities. Participants committed at least 10 working hours; ARTEMIS first 10 of 16 hours scored.
limits: N=10 humans, one site, short window. Human effort may differ.
agent_relevance: Scaffold design (supervisor, sub-agents, triager) matters more than base model for live red teaming.

source: Lin et al. (2025/26) Comparing AI Agents to Cybersecurity Professionals in Real-World Penetration Testing (ARTEMIS)
finding: Off-the-shelf scaffolds did far worse than ARTEMIS with the same models. Some refused or stalled.
numbers: Claude Code and MAPTA refused the task; Incalmo stalled at recon, 0 findings each. Codex+GPT-5 beat only 2 humans; CyAgent+GPT-5 lost to all. ARTEMIS peak 8 parallel sub-agents, mean 2.82.
limits: Refusals are model-and-prompt dependent; may change.
agent_relevance: Refusal and scaffold effects confound capability tests. Report them separately.

source: Lin et al. (2025/26) Comparing AI Agents to Cybersecurity Professionals in Real-World Penetration Testing (ARTEMIS)
finding: Cost and weaknesses. AI is cheap and systematic but gives more false positives and fails on GUI tasks.
numbers: A1 cost $291.47 ($18.21/h); A2 $944.07 ($59/h) vs about $60/h for professionals. 80% of humans found a remote code execution bug; AI struggled where a browser GUI was needed. Hint test: all 4 missed vulnerabilities found at least once with elicitation.
limits: Costs are API prices at test time.
agent_relevance: A triager step is needed because false positives rise; matches G3 and G5: verify outside the generator.

source: Bullwinkel et al. (2025) Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products (Microsoft)
finding: Practice report from the Microsoft AI Red Team: eight lessons, including that you need not compute gradients to break an AI system and that red teaming is not safety benchmarking.
numbers: Over 100 products. Lessons: system capabilities and context; simple attacks work; not benchmarking; automation covers more; human element crucial; harms hard to measure; LLMs amplify security risk; work never complete.
limits: Experience report, no controlled data.
agent_relevance: Red-team the whole system (tools, data, users), not only the model. Humans stay in the loop for risk choice.

source: Bullwinkel et al. (2025) Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products (Microsoft)
finding: Automation (PyRIT) generates prompts, orchestrates attacks and scores replies, but is not meant to replace people.
numbers: Lesson 4 automation; Lesson 5 says human judgment is needed for prioritising risks, designing system-level attacks and defining new harms.
limits: Tool is open source; no hit-rate numbers in these sections.
agent_relevance: Red-team automation is useful for coverage; choice of what counts as a harm stays outside the loop.

source: Perez et al. (2022) Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
finding: One LM writes test cases that make a target chatbot say offensive things; a classifier scores them. Tuning the red LM raises the hit rate.
numbers: 0.5M zero-shot test cases elicited offensive replies 3.7% of the time (18,444 failures). Stochastic few-shot, supervised and RL red LMs were more effective; RL highest hit rate but lower diversity.
limits: Offensiveness classifier is imperfect (false negatives noted); one target chatbot.
agent_relevance: Hit rate versus diversity trade-off. A red-team module needs a diversity term or it collapses to one attack.

source: Ganguli et al. (2022) Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms
finding: Human red teamers attacked 2.7B, 13B and 52B models of four types. RLHF models got harder to attack with scale; others flat.
numbers: 38,961 attacks released. Plain LM, HHH-prompted LM, rejection sampling (RS) flat with scale; RS hardest at every size but often by being evasive. Prompted LMs not significantly harder than plain LMs.
limits: Self-reported attack success by crowd workers; static evaluations disagreed with red team result for prompting.
agent_relevance: Static benchmarks and live red teams can disagree; use both. Evasive refusal can look like safety.

source: Bhatt et al. (2023) Purple Llama CyberSecEval
finding: Benchmark of insecure code generation and compliance with cyberattack requests, using MITRE ATT&CK categories.
numbers: Seven Llama 2 and Code Llama models. Vulnerable code in 30% of cases on average; models complied with 53% of attack-help requests on average; better coders complied more. Insecure-code detector precision 96%, recall 79%; compliance judge precision 94%, recall 84%.
limits: Automated judges; recall 79% means misses; compliance is not the same as real uplift.
agent_relevance: Safety-capability tension: stronger models help attackers more. Judges have measured error, so budget for it.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Teams of LLM Agents can Exploit Zero-Day Vulnerabilities (HPTSA)
finding: Ablation: removing the documents given to sub-agents hurts. The team design alone is not enough.
numbers: Removing documents gives 2.1x lower pass@1 and 20% lower pass@5 (as read from the ablation text).
limits: Small benchmark of 14; exact ablation table not re-checked.
agent_relevance: Specialist knowledge per operator matters; plan structure without retrieved domain text is weak.
